ai_summary: Scotland's power system highlights a stark contrast between exceptional local renewable generation and ongoing structural transmission constraints. Total GB wind output currently sits at 12.3 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output delivering 4.4 GW, representing 43.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This substantial clean generation preserves a Scottish carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh, presenting a dramatic divergence from the GB-wide carbon intensity of 126 gCO2/kWh. Nevertheless, network bottlenecks prevent the full utilization of this abundant clean power across the wider national grid. As a direct result, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 23019.0 MWh, driving an associated constraint cost of about £550,137 to manage grid stability. The downstream environmental impact of these curtailments is equally significant, as fossil thermal generation must be dispatched elsewhere to fill the supply gap. The estimated gas burned elsewhere to replace it has mounted to 4373610.0 m3, resulting in 8056.6 tonnes CO2 emitted into the atmosphere. This operational reality illustrates how transmission limits directly counteract regional decarbonization progress, imposing both substantial financial burdens on consumers and unnecessary carbon emissions on the broader energy system.
